p: I walk to school with my dad. We cross the road at the lights. My friend Mia waits for me at the gate.
At recess we eat fruit and play. I like the monkey bars best. When the bell rings, we go back to class.
Our class went to the library today. I found a book about sharks. I will read it with my mum tonight.
Today we had a cross country race. I ran all the way to the end. My legs were tired but I was happy.
My teacher has a reading corner. It has cushions and lots of books. We sit there when we finish our work.
It was my turn to feed the class fish. I gave it a small pinch of food. The fish swam up to eat it.

p: This term our class started a worm farm. We feed the worms fruit scraps from the canteen and keep the soil damp. The worms turn the scraps into rich compost, which we use in our vegetable garden. It is a great way to reduce waste.

Last week Year 6 went on camp. We went canoeing, built a campfire and slept in cabins. On the last night we had a talent show. My group did a funny skit and everyone laughed. I can't wait to go on camp again.

Our school has a buddy program for the younger students. Every Thursday I read with my buddy, Leo, who is in Kindergarten. He likes books about dinosaurs. Helping him learn to read makes me feel like a good role model.

The swimming carnival was held at the local pool. I swam in the freestyle and backstroke races. I didn't win, but I beat my best time. My friends cheered for me from the stands, which made me swim even faster.

Our class wrote letters to the council asking for a new pedestrian crossing near the school. We explained that many students walk to school and the road is busy. The council wrote back and said they would look into it.

In science we investigated which materials keep ice frozen the longest. We wrapped ice cubes in foil, paper, cotton and bubble wrap. The ice wrapped in bubble wrap lasted the longest because the air pockets slowed down the heat.

s: Starting high school can feel overwhelming, but most students settle in within the first few weeks.
Using a planner helps you keep track of assignments, tests and sport training each week.
Our English class is analysing how authors build tension in short stories.
The science teacher reminded us to wear safety glasses whenever we use the Bunsen burners.
Group projects work best when everyone agrees on roles and deadlines from the beginning.
Asking a question in class is a sign of curiosity, not a sign of weakness.
Our school's debating team will argue that homework should be banned in primary school.
The library offers quiet study spaces and free access to online databases.
Students elected to the Student Representative Council meet with the principal every month.
Cyberbullying should always be reported to a trusted adult or teacher straight away.
Our history class visited the museum to see artefacts from ancient Egypt.
Learning a language other than English opens doors to new friendships and cultures.
Before an exam, revising a little each day is far more effective than cramming the night before.
Our geography assignment involves surveying how people travel to school.
The school musical requires actors, singers, set designers and a lighting crew.
In mathematics we are learning how to solve equations with unknown values.
A good friend listens without judging and respects your decisions.
The careers adviser encouraged us to explore subjects that genuinely interest us.
Our food technology class baked bread and learned how yeast makes dough rise.
Reflecting on feedback from teachers can help you improve your next assignment.
The school is introducing a phone-free policy during lessons and lunch breaks.
Wellbeing lessons teach strategies for managing stress and getting enough sleep.
Our robotics club is building a machine to compete in a regional challenge.
Citing your sources properly shows respect for other people's ideas and avoids plagiarism.
Peer tutoring allows older students to help younger ones with difficult topics.
p: Moving from primary school to high school brings many changes. Instead of staying with one teacher, students move between classrooms and have different teachers for each subject. The timetable can be confusing at first, and there are more assignments to manage. However, high school also offers new subjects, clubs and opportunities to make friends from other schools.

Effective study habits are built over time. Students who set aside regular time each day, remove distractions and break large tasks into smaller steps tend to achieve better results. It also helps to test yourself rather than simply rereading notes, because recalling information strengthens memory. Getting enough sleep is just as important as studying.

Our class debated whether school uniforms should be compulsory. The affirmative team argued that uniforms create a sense of belonging and reduce pressure to wear expensive clothes. The negative team claimed that uniforms limit self-expression and can be uncomfortable in hot weather. In the end, the adjudicator praised both teams for using clear evidence.

Friendships often change during the teenage years. As students develop new interests, they may drift apart from old friends and form new groups. This is a normal part of growing up, although it can be painful. Talking honestly, showing kindness and being open to different people can help everyone feel included during this period of change.

The school's environment club decided to tackle the problem of litter in the playground. Members collected and sorted rubbish for a week, then presented their data at assembly. They discovered that most of the waste came from food packaging. As a result, the canteen introduced reusable containers and the amount of litter dropped significantly.

Learning to give and receive feedback is an important skill. When commenting on a classmate's work, it is useful to mention something they did well, suggest one clear improvement and stay respectful. When receiving feedback, try not to take it personally. Instead, see it as information that can help you grow and do better next time.

s: Senior students must balance demanding coursework with part-time jobs, sport and family responsibilities.
Academic integrity requires students to submit their own work and acknowledge every source they have used.
Effective revision involves spaced practice, active recall and regular attempts at past examination papers.
Choosing senior subjects should be guided by genuine interest as well as possible career pathways.
The rise of generative artificial intelligence has prompted schools to rethink how they assess student writing.
A well-structured essay presents a clear thesis and supports it with carefully selected evidence.
Students who feel connected to their school community are more likely to stay engaged with learning.
Wellbeing programs encourage students to recognise early signs of stress and seek support before problems escalate.
Leadership roles in the final year offer valuable experience in communication, organisation and teamwork.
Critical thinking involves questioning assumptions, evaluating evidence and considering alternative points of view.
Many universities now consider portfolios and interviews alongside traditional entrance rankings.
Work experience placements allow students to test whether a career suits them before committing to further study.
Teachers often say that the most successful students are not always the most talented but the most persistent.
Collaborative learning can deepen understanding, provided every member of the group contributes meaningfully.
Procrastination is frequently driven by anxiety about failure rather than simple laziness.
Taking concise, organised notes during lectures makes later revision considerably more efficient.
Digital literacy includes the ability to judge whether an online source is reliable, biased or deliberately misleading.
The final examinations are important, but they do not determine a person's entire future.
Vocational education and training courses provide practical pathways into skilled trades and industries.
Mentoring programs connect students with professionals who can share advice about further study and work.
Some educators argue that homework in the senior years should focus on quality and reflection rather than volume.
Learning to manage time is perhaps the most transferable skill students develop during their final years at school.
Debating teaches students to construct logical arguments and respond calmly under pressure.
Schools increasingly recognise that sleep, exercise and nutrition have a direct effect on academic performance.
Graduation marks the end of one chapter, yet it also represents the beginning of greater independence.
p: The final years of secondary school are often described as the most demanding. Students face a heavy workload, important assessments and decisions about their futures, all while managing personal relationships and responsibilities outside school. Research suggests that students who maintain a healthy routine, including regular exercise and adequate sleep, generally cope better with pressure. Schools therefore emphasise balance, reminding students that wellbeing and achievement are closely connected rather than competing priorities.

Academic writing differs from everyday writing in several important ways. It requires a formal tone, precise vocabulary and a logical structure in which each paragraph develops a single idea that supports the overall argument. Claims must be backed by credible evidence and properly referenced. Developing these skills takes practice, but they are valuable well beyond school, as clear written communication is highly valued in almost every profession and field of study.

The growing use of artificial intelligence tools has sparked debate among educators. Some worry that students will rely on these tools to complete assignments without genuine understanding. Others argue that, used responsibly, artificial intelligence can support learning by providing explanations, feedback and practice questions. Many schools are developing policies that allow limited use while requiring students to demonstrate their own thinking through drafts, discussions and supervised tasks.

Choosing what to do after school can be daunting. University is a common pathway, but it is not the only one. Apprenticeships, traineeships and vocational courses offer practical training and the chance to earn an income while learning. Some students take a gap year to work, travel or volunteer before deciding. Career advisers encourage students to research a range of options and to remember that many people change direction several times during their working lives.

Resilience is the ability to adapt and recover when things go wrong. For senior students, setbacks might include a disappointing mark, a rejected application or a difficult period at home. Psychologists suggest that resilience can be strengthened by building supportive relationships, reframing negative thoughts and setting realistic goals. Importantly, resilience does not mean coping alone; knowing when to ask for help is one of its most valuable components.

Group assessment tasks are designed to develop collaboration, but they can also create frustration when contributions are unequal. Successful groups usually establish clear expectations at the outset, assign specific roles and set internal deadlines. Regular check-ins allow problems to be identified early. When conflict arises, addressing it directly and respectfully is more productive than allowing resentment to build. These experiences prepare students for workplaces where teamwork is essential.
